opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it comes down to the fact that natural systems aren't random. Anything that has survived the process of evolution, or more generally any pattern that persists in nature, has been shaped by some kind of selection process over long periods of time. And that process imposes structure. Take protein folding: in principle, the number of possible conformations a protein could take is astronomically large, far too many to brute-force. Yet in nature proteins fold in milliseconds. That tells you the energy landscape isn't arbitrary. It has been sculpted so the system can find its way to a stable configuration. And if nature can find that path efficiently, there's some learnable structure underlying it.

So my conjecture is that any pattern that can be generated or found in nature can be efficiently discovered and modeled by a classical learning algorithm. The search spaces look intractable on paper, but the real data lies on a much lower-dimensional manifold. A neural network can learn the shape of that manifold and then navigate it efficiently, rather than enumerating everything. That's essentially what we did with AlphaFold, and in a different domain with AlphaGo, where the space of Go positions is vastly larger than the number of atoms in the universe, yet the system learned to focus on the tiny fraction of moves that matter.

It also connects to some deep questions in computer science, things like P versus NP, and what's really tractable for classical systems. I think a lot of people assumed you'd need quantum computers to model quantum or biological systems properly. That may be true for some arbitrary, unstructured problems. But for the systems nature actually produces, which have been through this filtering process, I suspect classical Turing machines, and specifically learning systems, can go much further than we expected. It may even turn out that the boundary of what's efficiently modelable classically is a fundamental part of physics, almost a way of understanding reality as information. That's one of the things I'd most like to understand before I'm done.

r001.rationale: The response says learning systems capture structure that lets them navigate the relevant space efficiently, citing AlphaFold and AlphaGo as examples.

r002.rationale: It says evolution and other long-term selection processes impose structure on natural systems.

r003.rationale: It tentatively conjectures that patterns generated or found in nature can be efficiently discovered and modeled by classical learning algorithms.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it comes down to a conjecture I've had for a long time, which is that anything that evolution has found, or that nature has produced through some kind of optimization process, has structure to it. It's not random. And if it has structure, then in principle a learning system can discover that structure, given enough data and the right kind of inductive biases.

Think about protein folding, which is the example I always come back to. Proteins fold in a fraction of a second. Levinthal's paradox says that if you tried to search the conformational space exhaustively, it would take longer than the age of the universe. So nature has clearly found an efficient path through that space. The physics does it effortlessly. And that told us there must be a learnable mapping from sequence to structure, otherwise biology itself couldn't work. The question was just whether we had the right architecture and enough data to find it. With AlphaFold it turned out we did.

I think there's something deeper there too. Evolution is itself a kind of learning algorithm. It's slow, it's wasteful, it's operating over millions of years, but it's fundamentally a search process with selection. So the things it produces tend to live on relatively low-dimensional manifolds within what would otherwise be an astronomically large space. They're compressible, in a sense. And classical learning algorithms, gradient descent on neural networks, are very good at finding compressible structure when it exists. They're not good at memorizing noise.

Now, I'd say "efficiently" is doing a lot of work in your question. Part of what we've found is that you often need to bring in domain knowledge, the geometry of the problem, the symmetries, the constraints the physics imposes. It's not just throwing a generic transformer at everything. In AlphaFold, encoding things like equivariance and the attention over residue pairs mattered enormously. So the efficiency comes from a kind of partnership between what the learning algorithm can discover and what we already understand about the system.

And I'd actually go further. My hope, and it's partly a scientific bet, is that this extends beyond biology. If you believe the natural world has this kind of structure all the way down, and I think the success of physics suggests it does, then a lot of the great challenges in science, materials, chemistry, maybe eventually parts of fundamental physics, become problems that are tractable to the same kind of approach. That's really the core of what I've wanted to do since I started, use AI as the ultimate tool for understanding the world around us.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learned structure and AlphaFold, but does not mention AlphaGo or explain that learned environment models make search tractable in both systems.

r002.rationale: It says things produced by evolution or nature’s optimization processes have structure and are not random.

r003.rationale: It tentatively claims evolved structure can be learned, but does not clearly endorse the broader conjecture that anything evolved can be efficiently modeled; it qualifies the efficiency claim with a need for domain knowledge and suitable biases.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think part of the answer is that natural systems have a lot of structure. They’re not arbitrary collections of things interacting randomly. There are regularities, symmetries, and patterns that repeat across different scales, and learning algorithms can exploit those.

Evolution also has to work incrementally. It builds on what’s already there, and that can lead to reusable components and modular systems. So even when the underlying system is enormously complicated, there may be a much simpler description of the behavior you’re trying to predict.

But I’d be careful about saying that evolution guarantees efficient learnability. It doesn’t. Some natural processes may be computationally irreducible, or so sensitive to initial conditions that long-term prediction is practically impossible. And modeling a system at a useful level of abstraction is different from simulating every microscopic interaction.

So the interesting question is: where is the structure, and can we find the right representation to capture it? I think that’s a large part of what makes learning work.

r001.rationale: It discusses exploitable structure in natural systems but does not explain how learned environment models make search tractable in AlphaGo and AlphaFold.

r002.rationale: It links natural-system structure to evolution, saying evolution builds incrementally and can produce reusable components and modular systems.

r003.rationale: It explicitly cautions that evolution does not guarantee efficient learnability, so it does not endorse the conjecture that anything evolvable can be efficiently modeled.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think evolution gives us a reason to be optimistic, although it’s not a guarantee. These systems weren’t designed arbitrarily. They were shaped by processes operating in the physical world, with constraints on energy, time, and resources. So there may be a lot of structure that a learning algorithm can exploit.

Take proteins. In principle, the space of possible configurations is astronomically large. But real proteins don’t search that space exhaustively when they fold. The physics and the evolutionary history constrain what actually happens. The hope is that a learning system can discover enough of that structure to predict the outcome without simulating every microscopic interaction.

But I’d distinguish predicting something useful from modeling a system completely. You might be able to predict a protein’s structure efficiently while still finding its dynamics, or its interactions inside a cell, extremely difficult. So I wouldn’t claim that everything evolution produces must be efficiently learnable classically. I’d say evolution often leaves us with structure, and finding that structure is what makes learning possible.

r001.rationale: It discusses learning to predict protein structures, but does not explain how learned environment models make search tractable in AlphaGo and AlphaFold.

r002.rationale: It says natural systems have structure because evolutionary history and physical constraints shaped them.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says evolution is no guarantee and that not everything evolution produces must be efficiently learnable classically, rather than tentatively endorsing the conjecture.
